/-
  The Birthday Bound: Quantitative Collision Resistance
  =====================================================

  Collision resistance is not an all-or-nothing property: even an *ideal* random
  function `H : {1,…,q} → {1,…,n}` (a random oracle restricted to `q` distinct
  queries into an `n`-point digest space) has collisions with a probability that
  grows quadratically in the number of queries.  This **birthday bound** is the
  fundamental quantitative limit on the collision resistance of *any* hash
  function with an `n`-element output: no matter how good the design, roughly
  `√n` queries suffice to find a collision.

  This file develops the exact combinatorics and the classical upper bound:

  * `card_injective_assignments` — the number of collision-free assignments of
    `q` queries into `n` slots is exactly the descending factorial
    `n.descFactorial q` (via the cardinality of `Fin q ↪ Fin n`);
  * `noCollisionProb_eq_prod` — the exact no-collision probability
    `n^{\underline q}/n^q` equals the product `∏_{i<q} (1 - i/n)`;
  * `birthday_pigeonhole` — once `q > n`, a collision is *guaranteed*;
  * `one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub` — a Weierstrass/Bernoulli product inequality;
  * `birthday_collision_bound` — the headline upper bound: the collision
    probability is at most `q(q-1)/(2n)`.

  The union-bound flavour `q(q-1)/(2n)` is exactly why a `2b`-bit digest
  (`n = 2^{2b}`) is needed for `b`-bit collision security, the reason SHA-256's
  `256`-bit output targets a `128`-bit collision-resistance level.

  -- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
  HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): The exact no-collision probability of `q` ideal
  queries into `n` slots is `∏_{i<q}(1 - i/n)`, and this product is bounded below
  by `1 - q(q-1)/(2n)`, giving a clean quadratic collision upper bound — the
  birthday bound — independent of any structural assumption on the hash.

  EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): `card_injective_assignments` follows from
  `Fintype.card_embedding_eq`.  `noCollisionProb_eq_prod` rewrites the descending
  factorial as `∏ (n - i)` (`Nat.descFactorial_eq_prod_range`) and casts termwise
  to `∏ (1 - i/n)`.  The bound combines the induction-proved product inequality
  `one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub` with the Gauss sum `∑_{i<q} i = q(q-1)/2`.

  ANALYSIS (Analyst): The product inequality is the crux: `1 - ∑ aᵢ ≤ ∏(1 - aᵢ)`
  for `aᵢ ∈ [0,1]` needs both `0 ≤ ∏` and `∏ ≤ 1` in the inductive step, so both
  side conditions are load-bearing (dropping either breaks `nlinarith`).  The
  hypothesis `q ≤ n` is exactly where every factor `1 - i/n` stays in `[0,1]`;
  beyond it the pigeonhole theorem takes over and the probability collapses to 0.

  CRITIQUE (Critic): Non-vacuity — `birthday_pigeonhole` produces a *genuine*
  collision (a `≠`-pair with equal images), not a vacuous statement, and the
  bound theorem is stated over the honest range `q ≤ n` with a strictly
  informative right-hand side.  The exact-count and exact-probability theorems
  rule out an over-loose reading.

  SYNTHESIS (PI): exact collision-free count (descending factorial) ⇒ exact
  no-collision probability (product form) ⇒ birthday upper bound `q(q-1)/(2n)`,
  with pigeonhole guaranteeing collisions past `q = n`: a self-contained
  quantitative collision-resistance package complementing the structural
  Merkle–Damgård / Merkle-tree extraction theorems.
-/
import Mathlib
import Cryptography.MerkleDamgard

namespace Cryptography.Birthday

open Finset

/-- **Weierstrass / Bernoulli product inequality.** For weights `f i ∈ [0,1]`,
    `1 - ∑ f i ≤ ∏ (1 - f i)`.  Proved by induction; the inductive step needs
    both `0 ≤ ∏` and `∏ ≤ 1`. -/
theorem one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub (s : Finset ℕ) (f : ℕ → ℚ)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, 0 ≤ f i ∧ f i ≤ 1) :
    1 - ∑ i ∈ s, f i ≤ ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) := by
  classical
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp
  | @insert a s ha ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_insert ha, Finset.prod_insert ha]
      have hb := h a (Finset.mem_insert_self a s)
      have ih' := ih (fun i hi => h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi))
      have hprod_nonneg : 0 ≤ ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) :=
        Finset.prod_nonneg (fun i hi => by
          have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).2; linarith)
      have hprod_le_one : ∏ i ∈ s, (1 - f i) ≤ 1 :=
        Finset.prod_le_one
          (fun i hi => by have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).2; linarith)
          (fun i hi => by have := (h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)).1; linarith)
      nlinarith [hb.1, hb.2, ih', hprod_nonneg, hprod_le_one]

/-- The exact probability that `q` uniform independent queries into `n` slots are
    all distinct: `n^{\underline q}/n^q` where `n^{\underline q}` is the
    descending factorial (the number of injective assignments). -/
noncomputable def noCollisionProb (n q : ℕ) : ℚ :=
  (n.descFactorial q : ℚ) / (n : ℚ) ^ q

/-- **Exact collision-free count.** The number of injective (collision-free)
    assignments of `q` queries into `n` slots is the descending factorial
    `n.descFactorial q`. -/
theorem card_injective_assignments (n q : ℕ) :
    Fintype.card (Fin q ↪ Fin n) = n.descFactorial q := by
  simp [Fintype.card_embedding_eq]

/-- Gauss sum, cast to `ℚ`: `∑_{i<q} i = q(q-1)/2`. -/
theorem sum_range_cast (q : ℕ) : (∑ i ∈ range q, (i : ℚ)) = (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / 2 := by
  rcases q with _ | m
  · simp
  · have h2 := Finset.sum_range_id_mul_two (m + 1)
    have hc := congrArg (Nat.cast (R := ℚ)) h2
    push_cast at hc ⊢
    linarith [hc]

/-- **Exact no-collision probability as a product.** For `q ≤ n`,
    `noCollisionProb n q = ∏_{i<q} (1 - i/n)`. -/
theorem noCollisionProb_eq_prod (n q : ℕ) (hq : q ≤ n) :
    noCollisionProb n q = ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with hn | hn
  · subst hn; interval_cases q; simp [noCollisionProb]
  · have hn' : (n : ℚ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
    have hRHS : ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n)
        = (∏ i ∈ range q, ((n : ℚ) - i)) / (n : ℚ) ^ q := by
      rw [Finset.prod_congr rfl
        (fun i _ => by field_simp : ∀ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) = ((n : ℚ) - i) / n)]
      rw [Finset.prod_div_distrib, Finset.prod_const, Finset.card_range]
    rw [hRHS]; unfold noCollisionProb
    rw [Nat.descFactorial_eq_prod_range]; push_cast
    congr 1
    apply Finset.prod_congr rfl
    intro i hi
    rw [mem_range] at hi
    rw [Nat.cast_sub (by omega)]

/-- **Birthday pigeonhole.** Once the number of queries exceeds the digest space
    (`q > n`), a collision is unavoidable: some two distinct queries hash equal. -/
theorem birthday_pigeonhole (n q : ℕ) (hqn : n < q) (f : Fin q → Fin n) :
    ∃ i j, i ≠ j ∧ f i = f j := by
  apply Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt
  simpa using hqn

/-- **The birthday bound.** For `q ≤ n` queries into an `n`-element digest space,
    the probability of at least one collision is at most `q(q-1)/(2n)`.  This is
    the quantitative ceiling on collision resistance: to reach `b`-bit security
    (`q ≈ 2^b` queries safe) the digest space must satisfy `n ≈ 2^{2b}`. -/
theorem birthday_collision_bound (n q : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) (hq : q ≤ n) :
    1 - noCollisionProb n q ≤ (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / (2 * n) := by
  have hn' : (0 : ℚ) < n := by exact_mod_cast hn
  rw [noCollisionProb_eq_prod n q hq]
  have hWeier : 1 - ∑ i ∈ range q, ((i : ℚ) / n) ≤ ∏ i ∈ range q, (1 - (i : ℚ) / n) := by
    apply one_sub_sum_le_prod_one_sub
    intro i hi
    rw [mem_range] at hi
    exact ⟨by positivity, by rw [div_le_one hn']; exact_mod_cast (by omega : i ≤ n)⟩
  have hsum : ∑ i ∈ range q, ((i : ℚ) / n) = (q * (q - 1) : ℚ) / (2 * n) := by
    rw [← Finset.sum_div, sum_range_cast]; ring
  linarith [hWeier, hsum.ge]

end Cryptography.Birthday

/-
  Merkle *Tree* Collision-Resistance Preservation
  ===============================================

  The Merkle–Damgård construction (see `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard`) iterates a
  compression function *linearly* along a message.  The other canonical domain
  extender is the **Merkle tree**: a two-to-one compression function `h` is
  applied along a *binary tree*, hashing pairs of chaining values up to a single
  root.  Merkle trees underlie authenticated data structures, certificate
  transparency, and blockchains, and — like the linear chain — they *preserve
  collision resistance*.

  We prove the tree analogue of `md_collision_extract`: any collision of the tree
  hash on two trees of the **same shape** constructively yields a collision of
  the underlying two-input compression function `h`.  The proof is a structural
  induction over the common shape, splitting each internal node into "the two
  child digests already collide" versus "recurse into the differing subtree".

  This complements the linear result: collision resistance is preserved by *both*
  the sequential (MD) and the parallel (tree) domain extenders, from the *same*
  primitive assumption (`HasPairCollision`, the two-input version of
  `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision`).

  -- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
  HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): Collision resistance is preserved by the Merkle
  *tree* extender exactly as for the linear chain: a root collision on same-shape
  trees must be traceable to a two-input compression collision at some internal
  node.

  EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): Introduced `MTree`, `treeHash`, and a `SameShape`
  relation making the two trees structurally comparable.  `tree_collision_extract`
  is proved by induction on `SameShape`.  At an internal node either the pair of
  child digests already differs (immediate `HasPairCollision`), or the digests
  agree and, since the trees differ, a differing subtree is found by the IH.

  ANALYSIS (Analyst): The `SameShape` hypothesis is the tree analogue of the
  equal-length hypothesis in the linear case: without it, two structurally
  different trees can share a root without any node collision (e.g. a leaf whose
  value equals the root hash of a subtree).  The theorem is stated at that tight
  boundary.  Injectivity is not assumed: the reduction is purely extractive.

  CRITIQUE (Critic): Non-vacuity — `treeHash_injOn_shape` shows the contrapositive
  (no `h`-collision ⇒ tree hash injective on each shape), and `pair_collision_of_card`
  proves via pigeonhole that two-input compressions over a ≥2-element finite state
  always *have* a collision, so the extraction theorem is about *finding*, not
  *existence*.  The base case genuinely uses `hne` (equal leaves are equal trees).

  SYNTHESIS (PI): `MTree` + `treeHash` + `SameShape` + `tree_collision_extract`
  + injectivity corollary + pigeonhole inevitability form a self-contained
  Merkle-*tree* collision-resistance package, parallel to the Merkle–Damgård one.
-/
import Mathlib
import Cryptography.MerkleDamgard

namespace Cryptography.MerkleTree

variable {State : Type*}

/-- A binary Merkle tree with `State`-labelled leaves. -/
inductive MTree (State : Type*) where
  | leaf : State → MTree State
  | node : MTree State → MTree State → MTree State

/-- The Merkle tree hash: leaves carry their value, internal nodes apply the
    two-to-one compression function `h` to the digests of their two children. -/
def treeHash (h : State → State → State) : MTree State → State
  | .leaf s => s
  | .node l r => h (treeHash h l) (treeHash h r)

/-- A two-input compression function `h` has a *collision* when two distinct
    input pairs `(a,b) ≠ (c,d)` map to the same output.  This is the two-argument
    analogue of `Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision`. -/
def HasPairCollision (h : State → State → State) : Prop :=
  ∃ a b c d, (a, b) ≠ (c, d) ∧ h a b = h c d

/-- Two trees have the *same shape* when their branching structure matches,
    ignoring leaf values. -/
inductive SameShape : MTree State → MTree State → Prop
  | leaf (s t : State) : SameShape (.leaf s) (.leaf t)
  | node {l₁ r₁ l₂ r₂ : MTree State} :
      SameShape l₁ l₂ → SameShape r₁ r₂ →
      SameShape (.node l₁ r₁) (.node l₂ r₂)

@[simp] theorem treeHash_leaf (h : State → State → State) (s : State) :
    treeHash h (.leaf s) = s := rfl

@[simp] theorem treeHash_node (h : State → State → State) (l r : MTree State) :
    treeHash h (.node l r) = h (treeHash h l) (treeHash h r) := rfl

/-- `SameShape` is reflexive. -/
theorem SameShape.refl (t : MTree State) : SameShape t t := by
  induction t with
  | leaf s => exact SameShape.leaf s s
  | node l r ihl ihr => exact SameShape.node ihl ihr

/-- **Merkle-tree collision extraction.**
    Any collision of the tree hash on two distinct, *same-shape* trees yields an
    explicit collision of the two-input compression function `h`. -/
theorem tree_collision_extract (h : State → State → State)
    (t₁ t₂ : MTree State) (hshape : SameShape t₁ t₂) (hne : t₁ ≠ t₂)
    (hcol : treeHash h t₁ = treeHash h t₂) :
    HasPairCollision h := by
  induction hshape with
  | leaf s t =>
      simp only [treeHash] at hcol
      exact absurd (by rw [hcol]) hne
  | @node l₁ r₁ l₂ r₂ hl hr ihl ihr =>
      simp only [treeHash] at hcol
      by_cases hpair : (treeHash h l₁, treeHash h r₁) = (treeHash h l₂, treeHash h r₂)
      · rw [Prod.mk.injEq] at hpair
        obtain ⟨hlh, hrh⟩ := hpair
        by_cases hll : l₁ = l₂
        · by_cases hrr : r₁ = r₂
          · exact absurd (by rw [hll, hrr]) hne
          · exact ihr hrr hrh
        · exact ihl hll hlh
      · exact ⟨_, _, _, _, hpair, hcol⟩

/-- **Collision resistance is preserved (contrapositive form).**
    If the compression function has no collision, then the tree hash is injective
    on each fixed tree shape. -/
theorem treeHash_injOn_shape (h : State → State → State)
    (hh : ¬ HasPairCollision h) (t₁ t₂ : MTree State)
    (hshape : SameShape t₁ t₂) (hcol : treeHash h t₁ = treeHash h t₂) :
    t₁ = t₂ := by
  by_contra hne
  exact hh (tree_collision_extract h t₁ t₂ hshape hne hcol)

/-- **Collisions are inevitable (pigeonhole).**
    A two-input compression function over a finite state space with at least two
    elements necessarily has a collision: its domain `State × State` is strictly
    larger than its codomain.  Collision resistance is therefore a *computational*
    notion — collisions exist; the difficulty is finding them. -/
theorem pair_collision_of_card [Fintype State] (hcard : 1 < Fintype.card State)
    (h : State → State → State) : HasPairCollision h := by
  have hpos : 0 < Fintype.card State := by omega
  obtain ⟨p, q, hpq, hval⟩ := Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt
    (fun p : State × State => h p.1 p.2)
    (by simpa [Fintype.card_prod] using
      (by nlinarith : Fintype.card State < Fintype.card State * Fintype.card State))
  exact ⟨p.1, p.2, q.1, q.2, by simpa using hpq, hval⟩

/-- **Both domain extenders start from an unavoidable collision.**
    Over finite state/block types (state with `≥ 2` elements, blocks with `≥ 2`
    values), the *linear* Merkle–Damgård compression `f` and the *tree* two-input
    compression `h` each necessarily have a collision.  This ties the tree
    inevitability (`pair_collision_of_card`) to the linear one
    (`Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.compression_collision_of_card`), showing both
    constructions rest on the *computational* (find-the-collision) hardness, not
    on collisions being absent. -/
theorem collisions_inevitable_both {Block : Type*}
    [Fintype State] [Fintype Block] [Nonempty State]
    (hcard : 1 < Fintype.card State) (hB : 1 < Fintype.card Block)
    (f : State → Block → State) (h : State → State → State) :
    Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.HasCompressionCollision f ∧ HasPairCollision h :=
  ⟨Cryptography.MerkleDamgard.compression_collision_of_card hB f,
   pair_collision_of_card hcard h⟩

end Cryptography.MerkleTree

# Computational Evidence — Collision Resistance of Hash Domain Extenders

This note collects the small-case numerical checks performed before formalizing
the two Lean files `MerkleTreeCollision.lean` and `BirthdayCollisionBound.lean`.

## 1. Birthday bound: exact no-collision probability vs. the quadratic upper bound

For a random function into `n` slots queried `q` times, the exact no-collision
probability is `P_nc(n,q) = ∏_{i<q} (1 - i/n)` and the collision probability is
`1 - P_nc`. The formalized bound is `1 - P_nc ≤ q(q-1)/(2n)`.

Classic `n = 365` (the actual "birthday paradox"):

| q  | P_nc     | collision prob = 1 − P_nc | bound q(q−1)/(2·365) |
|----|----------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| 10 | 0.883052 | 0.116948                  | 0.123288             |
| 20 | 0.588562 | 0.411438                  | 0.520548             |
| 22 | 0.524305 | 0.475695                  | 0.632877             |
| 23 | 0.492703 | 0.507297                  | 0.693151             |
| 29 | 0.319031 | 0.680969                  | 1.112329             |

Observations:
- The collision probability first exceeds `1/2` at `q = 23` (0.5073), the
  textbook birthday number — a sanity check on `noCollisionProb_eq_prod`.
- The upper bound `q(q-1)/(2n)` dominates the true collision probability at every
  `q` in the table (e.g. `q=2`: `0.002740 ≥ 0.002740`, tight; `q=23`:
  `0.693 ≥ 0.507`), consistent with `birthday_collision_bound`.
- For `q > n` the product contains a zero factor, so `P_nc = 0`: a collision is
  certain. This is the qualitative statement proved by `birthday_pigeonhole`.

## 2. Exact collision-free counts (descending factorial)

The number of collision-free assignments of `q` queries into `n` slots equals
`n^{\underline q} = n·(n−1)···(n−q+1)`, formalized as `card (Fin q ↪ Fin n) =
n.descFactorial q`. For `n = 10`:

`descFactorial 10 q` for `q = 0..5`: `1, 10, 90, 720, 5040, 30240`.

These are the falling factorials of 10 — **OEIS A008279** (triangle of
`n!/(n−k)!`, arrangements/permutations of `n` things `k` at a time). The `n = 10`
row matches A008279 exactly, confirming the exact-count formalization.

## 3. Merkle-tree collision extraction — hand-checked small cases

Two same-shape trees over a toy compression `h a b = (a + b) mod 4` on
`State = ZMod 4`:

- `t₁ = node (leaf 0) (leaf 3)`, `t₂ = node (leaf 1) (leaf 2)`.
  Root hashes: `h 0 3 = 3` and `h 1 2 = 3` — equal, trees differ, and
  `(0,3) ≠ (1,2)` is a genuine pair collision of `h`. This is exactly the
  "digests already differ at the root" branch of `tree_collision_extract`.
- `t₁ = node (node (leaf 0) (leaf 1)) (leaf 3)`,
  `t₂ = node (node (leaf 2) (leaf 3)) (leaf 3)` with `h a b = (a+b) mod 4`:
  left subtree digests `h 0 1 = 1`, `h 2 3 = 1` collide while the right leaves
  match, illustrating the "recurse into the differing subtree" branch.

## 4. Inevitability (pigeonhole)

For any `h : State → State → State` with `|State| = m ≥ 2`, the domain
`State × State` has `m² > m` elements, so `h` cannot be injective and a pair
collision always exists (`pair_collision_of_card`). E.g. `m = 2`: `4 > 2`.
This confirms collision resistance is a *computational* (find-the-collision)
notion, never an information-theoretic absence of collisions.

All four checks are consistent with the formalized theorems; no counterexamples
were found in the sampled ranges.

# Future Directions — Collision Resistance of Hash Domain Extenders

This cycle established, with fully verified proofs, three complementary faces of
collision resistance for iterated hashing: the *linear* Merkle–Damgård extractor,
the *parallel* Merkle-tree extractor, and the *quantitative* birthday ceiling that
bounds any hash with a finite digest. The conjectures below are the natural next
steps suggested by that work. Each is stated so that a single decisive example or
counterexample would settle it.

## 1. A universal extraction law for tree-shaped domain extenders

**Conjecture.** Every domain extender built by applying a fixed two-input
compression function along an *arbitrary* directed acyclic combining schedule
(not only balanced binary trees, but skew trees, Merkle–Patricia tries, and
sponge-like absorbing graphs) preserves collision resistance: any collision on
two inputs sharing the same combining schedule can be traced, in time linear in
the schedule size, to a collision of the compression function.

The key insight is that collision extraction is a purely *local* property of the
combining graph — a root collision must be witnessed at some internal node where
two distinct digest pairs meet — so the same node-by-node descent that works for
balanced trees should work for any acyclic schedule, with the schedule playing
the role that "equal length" and "same shape" play in the linear and binary-tree
cases.

Why now? Modern authenticated data structures (certificate-transparency logs,
blockchain state tries, verkle trees) use exactly these irregular combining
schedules, yet their collision-resistance guarantees are argued informally per
construction; a single graph-level theorem would cover them uniformly.

## 2. The shape hypothesis is exactly necessary

**Conjecture.** For the binary Merkle-tree hash there is a sharp dichotomy: two
inputs of the *same* shape collide only via a compression collision, but for
every compression function that is not injective in its combined argument there
exist two *different-shaped* trees that collide with **no** internal compression
collision at all. In other words, "same shape" is not a convenience hypothesis —
it is the precise boundary of extractability.

The key insight is that a shape mismatch lets a whole subtree's digest be
compared against a bare leaf value, so the collision can be absorbed entirely by
the shape ambiguity rather than by any pair of equal compression outputs; making
the extender safe therefore requires domain separation that encodes shape (length
and branching) into the input, mirroring the prefix-free padding that repairs the
linear construction.

Why now? Length-extension and shape-ambiguity attacks on real deployments (from
the classic Merkle–Damgård length-extension to tree-hash confusion in signature
schemes) keep re-appearing; pinning down that shape-encoding is *necessary and
sufficient* would turn a folklore rule of thumb into a design invariant.

## 3. Second-order birthday bounds for structured query sets

**Conjecture.** When the `q` queries to an ideal `n`-slot hash are not arbitrary
but are themselves drawn from a low-complexity structured family (an arithmetic
progression of messages, or the leaves of a fixed tree schedule), the collision
probability is still bounded by `q(q-1)/(2n)` and, more sharply, the *expected*
number of colliding pairs is exactly `q(q-1)/(2n)` regardless of the structure —
structure can cluster collisions but cannot increase their expected count.

The key insight is that the expected number of collisions is a sum of pairwise
indicator expectations, each exactly `1/n` by symmetry of the ideal function, so
the total is `binom(q,2)/n` independent of any correlation among the queries;
structure affects only the variance, i.e. how collisions bunch together, not
their mean.

Why now? Attack models increasingly exploit *structured* query sets (rebound and
differential collision attacks steer inputs along algebraic paths); separating
the "mean is structure-free" phenomenon from the "variance is structure-driven"
phenomenon would sharpen both attack analysis and provable-security margins.

## 4. Digest-length law from the birthday ceiling

**Conjecture.** The birthday bound is asymptotically tight in the strongest
sense: for every `n` there is a query budget `q(n) = Θ(√n)` at which the collision
probability crosses any fixed threshold `p ∈ (0,1)`, and the crossing point
scales as `q ≈ √(2n · ln(1/(1-p)))`. Consequently a digest space of size `n` can
support at most `Θ(log₂ n / 2)` bits of collision security — never more.

The key insight is that the exact product `∏(1 - i/n)` is squeezed between two
Gaussian-tail estimates `exp(-q²/(2n))`-style bounds, so its half-life in `q`
sits at a universal constant multiple of `√n`, making the `2b`-bit-output-for-
`b`-bit-security rule a theorem rather than a heuristic.

Why now? Post-quantum standardization is actively choosing digest lengths under
competing cost pressures; a tight two-sided law converting output size directly
into an achievable security level would remove guesswork from those choices.

# Algebraic Theory of L-Function Germs

This module formalizes the algebraic theory of *germs* of L-functions at `s = 1`,
providing the structural results that underlie the analytic side of the
Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture framework.

An L-function germ is modelled by the Taylor data of `L(s)` at `s = 1`, i.e. a
sequence of real coefficients `coeffs n` so that (formally)
`L(s) = ∑ n, coeffs n * (s - 1) ^ n`, together with a radius-of-convergence
guarantee.  The two invariants of central interest are:

* the **analytic rank** — the order of vanishing at `s = 1`, and
* the **leading coefficient** — the first nonzero Taylor coefficient.

The main structural results are that the analytic rank is *additive* and the
leading coefficient is *multiplicative* under the Rankin–Selberg style product
(the Cauchy product of Taylor coefficients).  These connect to the Selberg-class
degree bookkeeping in `Shared.SelbergClassCensus`.

## Notes on the statements

Two of the statements requested in the informal problem description are, taken
literally, *false*, and have been corrected here (the corrections are documented
at each theorem):

* `analyticRank_mul` requires non-vanishing hypotheses on `f` and `g`.
  Without them the all-zero germ (which has rank `0` by the degenerate
  convention) is a counterexample: if `f ≡ 0` and `g` has rank `3`, then
  `f · g ≡ 0` has rank `0 ≠ 0 + 3`.

* `selbergDegree_convolution` cannot hold as an *equality of degrees* with the
  convention `selbergDegree f = 2 * analyticRank f + 1`, because of a parity
  mismatch: `2·(r+s)+1 ≠ (2r+1)+(2s+1) = 2·(r+s)+2`.  The correct additive
  relation, proved below, is
  `selbergDegree (germMul f g) + 1 = selbergDegree f + selbergDegree g`.
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset BigOperators

open scoped Classical

namespace LFunctionGerm

/-- The germ of an L-function at `s = 1`, recorded through its Taylor data.

`coeffs n` is the `n`-th Taylor coefficient, so that formally
`L(s) = ∑ n, coeffs n * (s - 1) ^ n`. -/
structure _root_.LFunctionGerm where
  /-- The Taylor coefficients of `L` at `s = 1`. -/
  coeffs : ℕ → ℝ
  /-- Each coefficient is either zero or nonzero (a decidability witness used to
  extract the order of vanishing). -/
  wellDefined : ∀ n, coeffs n = 0 ∨ coeffs n ≠ 0
  /-- The Taylor series has a positive radius of convergence. -/
  converges : ∃ ε > 0, Summable (fun n => ‖coeffs n‖ * ε ^ n)

end LFunctionGerm

/-- A germ is *zero* when all of its Taylor coefficients vanish. -/
def LFunctionGerm.IsZero (f : LFunctionGerm) : Prop := ∀ n, f.coeffs n = 0

/--
A germ is nonzero iff it has some nonzero Taylor coefficient.
-/
theorem LFunctionGerm.not_isZero_iff (f : LFunctionGerm) :
    ¬ f.IsZero ↔ ∃ n, f.coeffs n ≠ 0 := by
  unfold LFunctionGerm.IsZero; aesop;

/-- The **analytic rank** (order of vanishing at `s = 1`): the least index with a
nonzero Taylor coefficient, or `0` for the degenerate all-zero germ. -/
noncomputable def analyticRank (f : LFunctionGerm) : ℕ :=
  if h : ∃ n, f.coeffs n ≠ 0 then Nat.find h else 0

/-- The **leading coefficient**: the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. -/
noncomputable def leadingCoeff (f : LFunctionGerm) : ℝ := f.coeffs (analyticRank f)

/--
The Cauchy product of two germs is summable with a positive radius of
convergence.  This is the analytic content of `germMul.converges`, isolated so it
can be reused.
-/
theorem cauchy_prod_converges (fc gc : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hf : ∃ ε > 0, Summable (fun n => ‖fc n‖ * ε ^ n))
    (hg : ∃ ε > 0, Summable (fun n => ‖gc n‖ * ε ^ n)) :
    ∃ ε > 0, Summable
      (fun n => ‖∑ p ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, fc p.1 * gc p.2‖ * ε ^ n) := by
  obtain ⟨ ε₁, hε₁, h₁ ⟩ := hf
  obtain ⟨ ε₂, hε₂, h₂ ⟩ := hg
  set ε := min ε₁ ε₂ with hε;
  -- Define `F : ℕ → ℝ := fun n => fc n * ε ^ n` and `G : ℕ → ℝ := fun n => gc n * ε ^ n`.
  set F : ℕ → ℝ := fun n => fc n * ε ^ n
  set G : ℕ → ℝ := fun n => gc n * ε ^ n;
  -- Since $F$ and $G$ are summable, their Cauchy product is also summable.
  have h_cauchy : Summable (fun n => ‖∑ p ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, F p.1 * G p.2‖) := by
    have h_cauchy : Summable (fun n => ‖F n‖) ∧ Summable (fun n => ‖G n‖) := by
      simp +zetaDelta at *;
      exact ⟨ Summable.of_nonneg_of_le ( fun n => by positivity ) ( fun n => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( pow_le_pow_left₀ ( by positivity ) ( by rw [ abs_of_nonneg ( by positivity ) ] ; exact min_le_left _ _ ) _ ) ( by positivity ) ) h₁, Summable.of_nonneg_of_le ( fun n => by positivity ) ( fun n => mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( pow_le_pow_left₀ ( by positivity ) ( by rw [ abs_of_nonneg ( by positivity ) ] ; exact min_le_right _ _ ) _ ) ( by positivity ) ) h₂ ⟩;
    convert summable_norm_sum_mul_antidiagonal_of_summable_norm h_cauchy.1 h_cauchy.2 using 1;
  -- By definition of $F$ and $G$, we have $\sum_{p \in \text{antidiagonal}(n)} F(p.1) G(p.2) = \varepsilon^n \sum_{p \in \text{antidiagonal}(n)} fc(p.1) gc(p.2)$.
  have h_cauchy_def : ∀ n, ∑ p ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, F p.1 * G p.2 = ε ^ n * ∑ p ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, fc p.1 * gc p.2 := by
    intro n; rw [ Finset.mul_sum _ _ _ ] ; refine' Finset.sum_congr rfl fun p hp => _
    rw [ Finset.mem_antidiagonal ] at hp; rw [ ← hp ] ; ring;
  simp_all +decide [ mul_comm ];
  exact ⟨ |min ε₁ ε₂|, abs_pos.mpr ( ne_of_gt ( lt_min hε₁ hε₂ ) ), h_cauchy ⟩

/-- The product of two germs, defined via the Cauchy product of Taylor
coefficients: `(f · g).coeffs n = ∑_{i+j=n} f.coeffs i * g.coeffs j`. -/
noncomputable def germMul (f g : LFunctionGerm) : LFunctionGerm where
  coeffs := fun n => ∑ p ∈ Finset.antidiagonal n, f.coeffs p.1 * g.coeffs p.2
  wellDefined := fun _ => Classical.em _
  converges := cauchy_prod_converges f.coeffs g.coeffs f.converges g.converges

/--
Below the analytic rank, all Taylor coefficients vanish.
-/
theorem coeffs_eq_zero_of_lt_analyticRank (f : LFunctionGerm) {n : ℕ}
    (h : n < analyticRank f) : f.coeffs n = 0 := by
  unfold analyticRank at h;
  split_ifs at h <;> simp_all +decide

/--
For a nonzero germ, the coefficient at the analytic rank is nonzero;
equivalently the leading coefficient is nonzero.
-/
theorem coeffs_analyticRank_ne_zero (f : LFunctionGerm) (hf : ¬ f.IsZero) :
    f.coeffs (analyticRank f) ≠ 0 := by
  have h : ∃ n, f.coeffs n ≠ 0 := (f.not_isZero_iff).mp hf
  simp only [analyticRank, dif_pos h]
  exact Nat.find_spec h

/--
The `(r+s)`-th Cauchy-product coefficient is `f_r * g_s`, where `r`, `s` are
the analytic ranks.  All cross terms vanish by `coeffs_eq_zero_of_lt_analyticRank`.
-/
theorem germMul_coeff_add (f g : LFunctionGerm) :
    (germMul f g).coeffs (analyticRank f + analyticRank g)
      = f.coeffs (analyticRank f) * g.coeffs (analyticRank g) := by
  unfold germMul;
  have h_sum : ∀ p ∈ antidiagonal (analyticRank f + analyticRank g), p ≠ (analyticRank f, analyticRank g) → f.coeffs p.1 * g.coeffs p.2 = 0 := by
    intro p hp hp'; rcases lt_trichotomy p.1 ( analyticRank f ) with h | h | h <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.mem_antidiagonal ] ;
    · exact Or.inl ( coeffs_eq_zero_of_lt_analyticRank f h );
    · grind;
    · exact Or.inr ( coeffs_eq_zero_of_lt_analyticRank g ( by linarith ) );
  convert Finset.sum_eq_single ( ( analyticRank f, analyticRank g ) ) _ _ <;> aesop

/--
Below `r + s`, every Cauchy-product coefficient vanishes.
-/

    (h : n < analyticRank f + analyticRank g) : (germMul f g).coeffs n = 0 := by
  convert Finset.sum_eq_zero _;
  rotate_left;
  exact ℕ × ℕ;
  exact Finset.antidiagonal n;
  exact fun p => f.coeffs p.1 * g.coeffs p.2;
  · intro p hp; by_cases h : p.1 < analyticRank f <;> by_cases h' : p.2 < analyticRank g <;> simp_all +decide [ coeffs_eq_zero_of_lt_analyticRank ] ;

This note records the small-case checks that guided the theorems in

## 1. Congruent numbers: small cases

A positive integer `n` is *congruent* if it is the area of a right triangle with
rational sides. First congruent numbers (OEIS **A003273**, "congruent numbers"):

```
5, 6, 7, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30, 31, 34, 37, 38, 39, ...
```

Witnesses used / checked:

| n  | (a, b, c)                       | a²+b²=c² | a·b/2 |
|----|---------------------------------|----------|-------|
| 6  | (3, 4, 5)                       | 25       | 6     |
| 5  | (3/2, 20/3, 41/6)               | ✓        | 5     |
| 7  | (35/12, 24/5, 337/60)           | ✓        | 7     |
| 30 | (5, 12, 13)                     | 169      | 30    |

`n = 6` with the 3–4–5 triangle is used as the non-vacuity anchor
(`six_isCongruent`).

Non-congruent small cases (unconditionally known): `1, 2, 3, 4`. In particular
Fermat's theorem that `1` is not congruent is equivalent to `y² = x³ − x` having only
the three `2`-torsion points — consistent with the curve-point map producing only
`y = 0` points there.

## 2. Fibonacci's three-squares-in-arithmetic-progression dictionary

For `n = 6`, the triangle (3,4,5) gives the arithmetic progression of rational squares
with common difference 6 and middle `(c/2)² = (5/2)² = 25/4`:

```
x − n = ((a−b)/2)² = (1/2)² = 1/4
x     = (c/2)²      = 25/4
x + n = ((a+b)/2)² = (7/2)² = 49/4
```

Check: `25/4 − 1/4 = 6` and `49/4 − 25/4 = 6`. All three are rational squares
(`1/4 = (1/2)²`, `25/4 = (5/2)²`, `49/4 = (7/2)²`). This is exactly the content of
`congruent_iff_threeSquareAP`, verified here on the smallest case.

For `n = 6`, `(a,b,c) = (3,4,5)`: `c − a = 2`,
`x = 6·4/2 = 12`, `y = 2·36/2 = 36`. Then

```
x³ − n²x = 12³ − 36·12 = 1728 − 432 = 1296 = 36² = y².   ✓  (y ≠ 0)
```

So `(12, 36)` is a rational point of infinite order on `y² = x³ − 36x`, confirming
`congruent_gives_curve_point` numerically.

Why now? Databases of elliptic curves organized by conductor make it possible to test,

**Conjecture.** Whenever an arithmetic L-function factors as a product of two
independent pieces, the order of vanishing at the central point is *exactly* the sum of
the two orders, with **no** cancellation — and this rigidity extends to the leading
coefficients, which multiply. Consequently, a factor can lower the central rank of a
product only by literally contributing zero order, never by interfering destructively.

The key insight is that the order of vanishing behaves like a valuation on the
multiplicative monoid of central germs: the lowest surviving term of a Cauchy product is
a single, non-cancelling product of the two leading terms because the coefficient field
has no zero divisors.

Why now? Rankin–Selberg convolutions and Artin factorizations are being computed at
scale, so the additivity-with-no-cancellation prediction can be checked directly against
tables of central orders and leading terms for products of degree-1 and degree-2

(order of torsion)²` is a class invariant, and this single constraint, combined with the

coefficient, so the entire arithmetic quotient above is forced to coincide across the

/-!
# Unimodularity of Figurate-Number Binomial Matrices

This file studies the family of Hankel-type integer matrices whose `(i, j)` entry is a
binomial coefficient of the form `C(c + i - j, n - 1)` (a "figurate number").  The central
result is that such a matrix is **unimodular**: its determinant is `±1`.

The proof is a fully constructive `LU`-style factorisation of the matrix into three
*unitriangular* matrices, each of determinant `1`.  Concretely, writing `C` for `Nat.choose`,
we exhibit

  `M = P * U * S0`

where

* `P i k  = C(i, k)`                    (lower unitriangular, Pascal matrix),
* `U k q  = C(c+1-n, q-k)`  for `k ≤ q` (upper unitriangular),
* `S0 q j = C(n-1-j, n-1-q)`           (lower unitriangular).

The two entrywise identities `P * U = T` and `T * S0 = M`, where `T i q = C(i + (c+1-n), q)`,
are each an instance of **Vandermonde's convolution identity** (`Nat.add_choose_eq`).

## Main results

* `FigurateBinomial.Mmat_det`      : `det (C(c+i-j, n-1))ᵢⱼ = 1` when `n - 1 ≤ c`.
* `FigurateBinomial.figurate_det`  : the actual figurate matrix `C(ℓ+n-i-j, n-1)` has
  determinant `(-1)^(n*(n-1)/2)` when `n - 1 ≤ ℓ + 1`.
* `FigurateBinomial.figurate_unimodular` : that determinant is a unit of `ℤ` (unimodularity).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The determinant of the figurate binomial matrix is identically 1.
Experiment (Experimenter): Direct computation over `n = 1..7`, all valid `ℓ`, and all
  `2 ≤ m ≤ n` showed the determinant is `(-1)^(n(n-1)/2)`, i.e. `±1` (NOT identically 1), and
  is `1` only for even `⌊n/2⌋`.  Moreover for `m < n` the genuine (non-truncated) figurate
  matrix is *singular* (rank ≤ m): only the top order `m = n` yields a unimodular matrix.
Analysis (Analyst): The "identically 1" claim is FALSE; the correct invariant is
  unimodularity with sign `(-1)^(n(n-1)/2)`.  After reversing the rows (a permutation of
  sign `(-1)^(n(n-1)/2)`) the matrix `C(ℓ+n-i-j,n-1)` becomes `C(c+i-j,n-1)` with `c = ℓ+1`,
  whose determinant is exactly `1`.  This reduced matrix factors as `P·U·S0`, three
  unitriangular matrices, by two applications of Vandermonde's convolution.
Critique (Critic): The factorisation is only valid when `n-1 ≤ c` (equivalently `n-2 ≤ ℓ`),
  otherwise `ℕ`-truncated subtraction corrupts `c+1-n`; this hypothesis is retained and is
  exactly the threshold at which all entries are genuine binomials.
Synthesis (PI): Unimodularity = product of unitriangular determinants; the sign of the
  figurate matrix is the sign of the row-reversal permutation.
-/

open Matrix Finset

namespace FigurateBinomial

/-- Pascal lower-triangular matrix, `P i k = C(i, k)`. -/
def Pmat (n : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun i k => (Nat.choose i k : ℤ)

/-- Upper-triangular convolution matrix, `U k q = C(c+1-n, q-k)` for `k ≤ q`, else `0`. -/
def Umat (n c : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun k q => if (k : ℕ) ≤ q then (Nat.choose (c + 1 - n) (q - k) : ℤ) else 0

/-- Lower-triangular matrix `S0 q j = C(n-1-j, n-1-q)`. -/
def S0mat (n : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun q j => (Nat.choose (n - 1 - j) (n - 1 - q) : ℤ)

/-- Intermediate matrix `T i q = C(i + (c+1-n), q)`. -/
def Tmat (n c : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun i q => (Nat.choose (i + (c + 1 - n)) q : ℤ)

/-- The reduced figurate binomial matrix, `M i j = C(c + i - j, n - 1)`. -/
def Mmat (n c : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun i j => (Nat.choose (c + i - j) (n - 1) : ℤ)

/-- The actual figurate binomial matrix, `F i j = C(ℓ + n - i - j, n - 1)`. -/
def Fmat (n l : ℕ) : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ :=
  fun i j => (Nat.choose (l + n - i - j) (n - 1) : ℤ)

/-
`P` is lower triangular.
-/
lemma Pmat_det (n : ℕ) : (Pmat n).det = 1 := by
  rw [ ← Matrix.det_transpose, Matrix.det_of_upperTriangular ];
  · simp +decide [ Pmat ];
  · intro i j hij; simp_all +decide [ Pmat ] ;
    exact Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt hij

/-
`U` is upper triangular with unit diagonal.
-/
lemma Umat_det (n c : ℕ) : (Umat n c).det = 1 := by
  convert Matrix.det_of_upperTriangular _;
  all_goals try infer_instance;
  · -- By definition of $Umat$, we know that $Umat n c i i = 1$ for all $i$.
    simp [Umat];
  · intro i j hij; unfold Umat; aesop;

/-
`S0` is lower triangular with unit diagonal.
-/
lemma S0mat_det (n : ℕ) : (S0mat n).det = 1 := by
  rw [ ← Matrix.det_transpose, Matrix.det_of_upperTriangular ];
  · simp +decide [ S0mat ];
  · intro i j hij; simp_all +decide [ S0mat ] ;
    rw [ Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt ( by omega ) ]

/-
First Vandermonde convolution: `P * U = T`.
-/
lemma PU_eq_T (n c : ℕ) : Pmat n * Umat n c = Tmat n c := by
  ext i j;
  simp +decide [ Pmat, Umat, Tmat, Matrix.mul_apply ];
  rw_mod_cast [ Nat.add_choose_eq ];
  rw [ ← Finset.sum_filter ];
  refine' Finset.sum_bij ( fun x hx => ( x, j - x ) ) _ _ _ _ <;> simp +decide [ Finset.mem_filter ];
  · exact fun a ha => Nat.add_sub_of_le <| mod_cast ha;
  · exact fun a₁ a₂ h₁ h₂ h₃ h₄ => Fin.ext h₃;
  · exact fun a b h => ⟨ ⟨ a, by linarith [ Fin.is_lt j ] ⟩, Nat.le_of_lt_succ ( by linarith [ Fin.is_lt j ] ), rfl, by simp +decide [ ← h ] ⟩

/-
Second Vandermonde convolution: `T * S0 = M`, valid when `n - 1 ≤ c`.
-/
lemma TS0_eq_M (n c : ℕ) (hc : n - 1 ≤ c) : Tmat n c * S0mat n = Mmat n c := by
  ext i j; simp +decide [ *, Matrix.mul_apply ] ;
  have h_vandermonde : (Nat.choose (i + (c + 1 - n) + (n - 1 - j)) (n - 1) : ℤ) = ∑ q ∈ Finset.range n, (Nat.choose (i + (c + 1 - n)) q : ℤ) * (Nat.choose (n - 1 - j) (n - 1 - q) : ℤ) := by
    rw_mod_cast [ Nat.add_choose_eq ];
    rcases n <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.Nat.sum_antidiagonal_eq_sum_range_succ_mk ];
    exact Fin.elim0 i;
  convert h_vandermonde.symm using 1;
  · rw [ Finset.sum_range ] ; rfl;
  · exact congr_arg _ ( congr_arg₂ _ ( by omega ) rfl )

/-- **Reduced figurate determinant.** The matrix `C(c+i-j, n-1)` has determinant `1`
whenever `n - 1 ≤ c`. -/
theorem Mmat_det (n c : ℕ) (hc : n - 1 ≤ c) : (Mmat n c).det = 1 := by
  have h : Mmat n c = (Pmat n * Umat n c) * S0mat n := by
    rw [PU_eq_T, TS0_eq_M n c hc]
  rw [h, Matrix.det_mul, Matrix.det_mul, Pmat_det, Umat_det, S0mat_det, mul_one, mul_one]

/-
The figurate matrix is the reduced matrix with its rows reversed.
-/
lemma Fmat_eq_submatrix (n l : ℕ) (hl : n - 1 ≤ l + 1) :
    Fmat n l = (Mmat n (l + 1)).submatrix (⇑(Fin.revPerm : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))) id := by
  ext i j; simp +decide [ Fmat, Mmat, Fin.revPerm ] ;
  grind +splitImp

/-
Sign of the row-reversal permutation on `Fin n`.
-/
lemma sign_revPerm (n : ℕ) :
    ((Equiv.Perm.sign (Fin.revPerm : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : ℤ)) = (-1) ^ (n * (n - 1) / 2) := by
  rcases n with ⟨ ⟩ <;> norm_num at *;
  · rfl;
  · simp +decide [ Fin.revPerm, Equiv.Perm.sign_eq_prod_prod_Iio ];
    rename_i n; rw [ Finset.prod_congr rfl fun i hi => Finset.prod_congr rfl fun j hj => by rw [ if_neg ( by exact not_lt_of_ge ( le_of_lt ( Finset.mem_Iio.mp hj ) ) ) ] ] ; norm_num;
    rw [ Finset.prod_pow_eq_pow_sum ];
    rw [ Finset.sum_fin_eq_sum_range ];
    norm_num [ Finset.sum_range_id ];
    rw [ Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x hx => if_pos <| Finset.mem_range_succ_iff.mp hx ] ; simp +decide [ mul_comm, Finset.sum_range_id ]

/-- **Figurate determinant.** The determinant of `C(ℓ+n-i-j, n-1)` is `(-1)^(n(n-1)/2)`
whenever `n - 1 ≤ ℓ + 1`. -/
theorem figurate_det (n l : ℕ) (hl : n - 1 ≤ l + 1) :
    (Fmat n l).det = (-1) ^ (n * (n - 1) / 2) := by
  rw [Fmat_eq_submatrix n l hl, Matrix.det_permute, Mmat_det n (l + 1) hl, mul_one]
  exact_mod_cast sign_revPerm n

/-- **Unimodularity.** The determinant of the figurate binomial matrix is a unit of `ℤ`. -/
theorem figurate_unimodular (n l : ℕ) (hl : n - 1 ≤ l + 1) :
    IsUnit (Fmat n l).det := by
  rw [figurate_det n l hl]
  exact (isUnit_one.neg : IsUnit (-1 : ℤ)).pow _

end FigurateBinomial

# Future Directions — Unimodular Binomial Hankel Matrices

Five falsifiable conjectures distilled from this research cycle. Each is stated to be
testable on small cases and provable (or refutable) by the same
factorisation-and-convolution machinery that settled the figurate case.

## 1. The order gap governs the rank of figurate Hankel matrices

**Conjecture.** For the `n × n` Hankel matrix whose entries are the `m`-dimensional
figurate numbers `C(a + i + j, m − 1)` (with the shift chosen so that every entry is a
genuine binomial coefficient), the rank equals `min(m, n)`. In particular the matrix is
invertible exactly when `m ≥ n`, and when `m = n` its determinant is the unit
`(−1)^(n(n−1)/2)`.

The key insight is that a figurate number of order `m` is a degree-`(m−1)` polynomial in
the index sum, so a Hankel matrix built from it inherits a linear recurrence of order `m`;
the determinant collapses to a single non-intersecting family of lattice paths precisely
when the matrix is square at the critical order `m = n`.

**Why now?** The critical-order phenomenon explains, in one stroke, both the unimodularity
at `m = n` and the singularity at `m < n` observed numerically, and it converts a delicate
determinant evaluation into a clean rank statement that finite differencing can certify.

## 2. Unimodularity is stable under arbitrary affine reindexing

**Conjecture.** Replacing the arithmetic index maps `i ↦ i`, `j ↦ j` by any two strictly
monotone affine maps with integer slopes `± 1` leaves the determinant of the top-order
figurate matrix equal to `± 1`; the sign is the product of the signs of the two induced
index permutations.

The key insight is that every such reindexing is a composition of a row/column reversal
(a permutation whose sign is `(−1)^(n(n−1)/2)`) with the unitriangular Pascal factorisation,
so the absolute value of the determinant is a permutation-invariant of the underlying
Vandermonde convolution rather than a property of the specific index labelling.

**Why now?** Reversing the rows was the single move that turned the "sign `± 1`" figurate
matrix into a "determinant exactly `1`" matrix; recognising this as one instance of a whole
symmetry group predicts a family of unimodular matrices useful as integer change-of-basis
templates.

## 3. Cholesky-unimodular binomial families are closed under Hadamard squaring

**Conjecture.** If a symmetric binomial Hankel matrix `H` admits a factorisation
`H = L Lᵀ` with `L` lower-unitriangular and integer, then the entrywise (Hadamard) square
`H ∘ H` also has determinant `1`.

The key insight is that the entrywise square of a Vandermonde-type convolution is again a
convolution — the squared binomial coefficients are the diagonal of a tensor product of two
Pascal matrices — so the Cholesky factor of `H ∘ H` can be assembled from Kronecker blocks
of the Cholesky factor of `H`.

**Why now?** Row-of-squares identities such as `Σ C(n,k)² = C(2n,n)` already appear as the
diagonal of the symmetric Pascal matrix; the conjecture asks whether that scalar identity is
the shadow of a full unimodular matrix identity, which would supply new integer lattices with
controlled determinants.

## 4. Determinant-one binomial matrices are a source of integer secret-sharing bases

**Conjecture.** Every top-order figurate matrix `C(c + i − j, n − 1)` (with `c ≥ n − 1`)
is the reduction modulo a prime `p` of an invertible matrix over `ℤ/pℤ` whose inverse has
entries bounded independently of `p`; hence it yields a public reconstruction basis for an
`(n, n)`-threshold linear scheme with no modular blow-up.

The key insight is that unimodularity over the integers forces invertibility over every
finite field simultaneously, and the explicit unitriangular factors give an inverse with
small, prime-independent integer entries — precisely the property a reconstruction matrix
needs to avoid leaking information through coefficient size.

**Why now?** Linear secret sharing increasingly needs public matrices that stay invertible
across many moduli; a determinant that is a fixed unit `± 1` (not merely a nonzero residue)
is the strongest possible such guarantee, and the figurate family provides infinitely many
concrete examples.

## 5. The alternating sign is the parity of a lattice-path crossing number

**Conjecture.** For the top-order figurate matrix, the sign `(−1)^(n(n−1)/2)` of the
determinant equals the parity of the total number of crossings in the unique family of
non-intersecting lattice paths that survives the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot expansion after
the rows are reversed.

The key insight is that reversing the rows converts a fully crossing path system into a
non-crossing one, and each elementary uncrossing flips the sign exactly once, so the global
sign is a combinatorial crossing invariant rather than an analytic accident.

**Why now?** Bijective proofs of binomial determinant evaluations (in the spirit of the
attached Gessel and Zeilberger references) have matured to the point where the sign, not just
the magnitude, can be read off a canonical path configuration — turning a parity computation
into a picture.

# Future Directions — Reciprocity through three lenses

This cycle assembled three structurally independent routes into quadratic
residuacity — cyclotomic Gauss sums, Eisenstein's lattice-point counting, and the
parity of the multiplication permutation (Zolotarev) — together with closed-form
proofs of both supplementary laws. The following conjectures are the natural,
falsifiable next steps suggested by that work.

## Conjecture 1 — Permutation-sign reciprocity for all odd moduli

For coprime odd numbers `m` and `n`, the product of Jacobi symbols
`(m/n)·(n/m)` equals the sign of the "grid-transpose" permutation of the
`m × n` array of residues induced by the Chinese Remainder correspondence, and this
sign is exactly `(-1)^((m-1)/2·(n-1)/2)`.

The key insight is that reading the residues of `ℤ/mnℤ` first row-by-row and then
column-by-column differs only by a permutation whose parity is a pure counting
invariant of the rectangle, so reciprocity becomes a statement about shuffling a
grid rather than about primes at all.

Why now? The permutation-sign characterization of the Legendre symbol is now on
firm footing, and it reduces the full reciprocity law to a single, self-contained
combinatorial parity — the cleanest possible target for the next push, and one that
automatically generalizes past primes to all odd moduli.

## Conjecture 2 — A unified sign functional across the three proofs

There is a single integer-valued invariant `Φ(a,p)`, definable simultaneously as a
Frobenius eigenvalue, as a lattice-point parity, and as a permutation sign, such
that all three classical proofs are instances of the identity `Φ(a,p) = (a/p)`, and
the equality of any two of the three descriptions is itself equivalent to a known
lattice identity.

The key insight is that the Gauss-sum, Eisenstein, and Zolotarev arguments are not
merely three proofs of one theorem but three evaluations of one functional, so their
pairwise agreements should encode genuine combinatorial identities in their own
right.

Why now? With all three mechanisms available in explicit, checkable form, their
outputs can be compared term-by-term for the first time, making the hunt for the
common functional a concrete search rather than a philosophical hope.

## Conjecture 3 — Higher supplementary laws in exponent form

For every fixed small integer `d`, the value `(d/p)` admits a closed exponent
formula `(-1)^(f_d(p))` where `f_d` is an explicit quadratic quasi-polynomial in the
residue of `p` modulo `4d`, and the period `4d` is optimal (no smaller modulus
works) precisely when `d` is squarefree.

The key insight is that the two classical supplements for `-1` and `2` are the first
two cases of a single family governed by the conductor of the quadratic character
attached to `d`, so their exponent shapes should persist with a predictable,
conductor-controlled period.

Why now? Having both supplements pinned to the exact exponents `(p-1)/2` and
`(p²-1)/8`, the pattern of "quadratic quasi-polynomial in `p mod 4d`" is visible and
testable against tables for `d = 3, 5, 6, 7`.

## Conjecture 4 — Cycle type detects the order of the residue

The full cycle type of the multiplication-by-`a` permutation on `ℤ/pℤ` is
determined by the multiplicative order `d` of `a`: it consists of `(p-1)/d` cycles
of length `d` (and one fixed point), so not only the sign but the entire conjugacy
class of the permutation is an arithmetic invariant of `a`, and `a` is a quadratic
residue if and only if `(p-1)/d` is even.

The key insight is that Zolotarev's sign is only the shadow of a finer object — the
orbit decomposition of the cyclic action — whose full shape recovers the order of
`a`, turning residuacity into a special case of a complete structural statement.

Why now? The sign computation already went through the cycle structure of a
generator; extending from "one cycle" to "the general orbit count" is the immediate
generalization and yields an order-detection criterion for free.

where `coverCount B S` is the number of blocks meeting `S` (so `coverCount B S / |B|` is the
per-draw probability of covering a new point of `S`, and `E[min_{p∈S} τ_p] = |B| / coverCount B S`).

* `fano_card` : there are `7` Fano lines.

# Future Directions: Structured Covers and Coupon-Collection Slowness

These conjectures are distilled from the cycle's findings: that a projective plane's line family
covers its point set strictly more slowly than genuinely uniform blocks of the same size, and that
the direction of every such "efficiency" statement is decided by the baseline against which it is
measured.

## Conjecture 1 — Projective planes are universally slow (the general-q statement)

For every prime power `q ≥ 2`, drawing uniformly random lines of the projective plane of order `q`
takes strictly longer, in expectation, to cover all `q²+q+1` points than drawing uniformly random
`(q+1)`-subsets of those points.

The key insight is that, for every fixed set `S` of points, the number of lines meeting `S` never
exceeds the number of `(q+1)`-subsets meeting `S`, with the two counts diverging most for the
subsets `S` that are unions of a few lines; this per-set domination survives the alternating
inclusion–exclusion sum and forces a strictly larger total cover time. Why now? The uniform side
now has an exact closed form as a single sum over subset sizes, so the whole problem reduces to a
size-by-size comparison of "lines meeting `S`" against "`(q+1)`-subsets meeting `S`" — a purely
combinatorial domination that is within reach of current design-theoretic counting.

## Conjecture 2 — Monotone efficiency along the block-structure ladder

Among all families of equal-size blocks on a fixed ground set, the expected cover time is a
monotone functional of how "spread out" the family is: the maximally spread family (all `k`-subsets)
is the fastest cover, and any balanced combinatorial design of the same block size is strictly
slower, with the deficit growing as the design's blocks overlap more regularly.

The key insight is that expected cover time is governed entirely by the coverage counts
`coverCount(B, S)`, and a family that maximises every one of these counts simultaneously minimises
every reciprocal in the inclusion–exclusion expansion; regular designs sacrifice coverage on exactly
the subsets that their blocks are engineered to hit repeatedly. Why now? The coverage-count identity
for uniform blocks isolates the single quantity through which block structure enters the cover time,
turning a probabilistic comparison into an extremal-set-systems inequality.

has its sign determined by the baseline: measured against one-coupon-per-draw collection, any
